synopsis: The corpus identifies Liu and Feng’s “Curse of rarity,” published in Nature Communications in 2024, as an on-road statistical validation precedent [f635, f426]. Its central explanation is that safety-critical events are rare and embedded in a very high-dimensional environment, making the distribution tail difficult to learn and validate [f635]. The glossary emphasizes that this testing difficulty increases as the number of variables grows [f13306]. Chapter 1 indicates that the tail remains difficult even in accelerated and rare-event statistical validation; the supplied facts do not quantify that difficulty or establish its applicability to heavy off-road machines [f353, f635, f426].

relations.note: Both explain difficult tail validation through high dimensionality.
Identifies authors, publication venue, and the rarity and dimensionality underlying tail-validation difficulty.
Increasing dimensionality explains persistent tail-testing difficulty.
Details the publication and argument of one listed on-road validation precedent.
